title: Growing Plant Records
statement:
A gardener measured a plant **n** times and wrote the numbers down in order. She wants to pick some of the measurements (keeping their original order, but skipping any she likes) so that the chosen values are **strictly increasing**.

What is the largest number of measurements she can pick? This is the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.
input:
The first line contains an integer **n**.

The second line contains n integers a[1], ..., a[n].
output: Print one integer: the length of the longest strictly increasing subsequence.

samples.explanation: The values must be strictly increasing, so equal values cannot both be picked.

hints: The O(n^2) DP: len[i] = 1 + max(len[j]) over j < i with a[j] < a[i]. It is correct but too slow for large n.
Keep an array tails[k] = the smallest possible last value of an increasing subsequence of length k + 1. It is always sorted, so you can binary search in it.
editorial:
Maintain `tails`, where `tails[k]` is the smallest value that can end a strictly increasing subsequence of length k + 1. For every x, find with binary search the first position with `tails[pos] ≥ x` (lower bound). If there is none, append x (we found a longer subsequence); otherwise replace `tails[pos]` by x (a smaller ending is always better). The length of `tails` is the answer. Using lower bound (not upper bound) is what makes the sequence strictly increasing.

Complexity: O(n log n).
